state.misconception_label: Confuses rest and movement on a distance time graph

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: This graph shows how far Fido the dog is from his home. What might the negative-sloping section represent? ![A graph with time (secs) on the horizontal axis and distance (m) on the vertical axis. The graph starts at the origin, travels in a straight line up and right, travels horizontally, then travels in a straight line down and right back to the x-axis. ](). I got Fido has fallen asleep because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: The negative-sloping section of the graph represents Fido moving away from his home. Remember, a negative slope on a distance-time graph means the object is moving in the opposite direction from its starting point. Make sure to pay attention to the direction of the line when analyzing distance-time graphs.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Wait, but I thought a negative slope meant he was going backwards? And if the line is going down, doesn't that mean the distance is getting smaller, so he's coming back towards his home, not going away from it?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: You are correct that a negative slope indicates the object is moving in the opposite direction from its starting point. In this case, Fido moving away from his home would result in a negative slope on the graph. Remember, the direction of the line on a distance-time graph is what determines the object's movement.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (claiming negative slope means moving away when it actually means returning home), ignores the student's correct reasoning in Turn 2, and simply restates the same incorrect claim without engaging with the student's valid objection.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher provides incorrect information (claiming negative slope means moving away when it actually means returning home) and fails to give explicit procedures, worked steps, or proper corrective feedback that would characterize rule-based instruction.
